desc:
Call a substring of s unique if it occurs in s exactly once (counting overlapping occurrences). Return the length of the shortest unique substring of s. The whole string is always unique, so an answer exists.

s = "banana"  ->  1   ("b" occurs once)
s = "abab"    ->  2   ("a", "b", "ab" occur twice, "ba" once)
s = "aaaa"    ->  4   ("a", "aa", "aaa" repeat, only "aaaa" is unique)
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: Counting all substrings of each length with a hash map is correct but costs O(n<sup>2</sup>) substrings, each of up to n characters.
A substring that occurs once is a prefix of exactly one suffix. Which prefixes of a suffix are shared with another suffix?

Sort the suffixes. A suffix is shared with others exactly up to its LCP with its sorted neighbours, so its shortest unique prefix has length max(lcp_left, lcp_right) + 1 (valid only if that does not exceed the suffix length). Take the minimum over all suffixes.
editorial: Any substring is a prefix of the suffix where it starts. In the sorted order of suffixes, all suffixes that share a given prefix form a contiguous block, so a prefix of suffix k of length L occurs again elsewhere exactly when L ≤ max(lcp[k-1], lcp[k]), where lcp is the neighbour LCP array. Hence the shortest unique prefix of suffix k has length max(lcp[k-1], lcp[k]) + 1, provided that is at most the suffix length (a suffix that is a prefix of its neighbour has none).

The answer is the minimum of these values over all suffixes. Build the suffix array and the LCP array as in the two earlier problems, then one pass finishes: O(n log<sup>2</sup> n) with prefix doubling and O(n) for the scan. An alternative is to binary search the length L and test with rolling hashes whether some window of length L occurs exactly once; this works because a unique substring of length L extends to a unique one of length L + 1.
